entry: American business executive and co-founder of [[Oracle Corporation]]. He served as Oracle's chief executive from 1977 to 2014 and has been its chief technology officer and executive chairman since 2014. He remains the largest shareholder of Oracle and of the mass media and entertainment conglomerate Skydance, which is managed by his son David Ellison. On September 10, 2025, he was briefly the world's wealthiest person after an increase in Oracle's stock price. He owns 98% of the land on [[Lānaʻi]], one of the Hawaiian Islands, and holds a stake in [[Tesla, Inc.]] worth over $19 billion.

American actor. Born in [[Fort Worth, Texas|Fort Worth]], he was best known for playing the ruthless oil baron J. R. Ewing in the primetime [[Soap opera|soap opera]] [[Dallas (TV series)|Dallas]] (1978–1991) and the astronaut Major Anthony Nelson in the sitcom *I Dream of Jeannie* (1965–1970). He had supporting roles in films including *Fail-Safe*, *Harry and Tonto*, *S.O.B.*, *Nixon* and *Primary Colors*, and also worked as a television producer and director. After a life-saving liver transplant in 1995, he became an advocate for organ donation and for environmental causes, including solar energy and opposition to nuclear power.

American television and radio host. Born Lawrence Harvey Zeiger in [[Brooklyn]], New York, he began in radio in Miami in 1957. From 1978 he hosted *The Larry King Show*, an all-night call-in program on the Mutual Broadcasting System. He hosted the nightly interview program *Larry King Live* on [[CNN]] from 1985 to 2010. From 2012 to 2020 he hosted *Larry King Now*, which ran on Hulu, Ora TV and RT America. King conducted over 50,000 interviews on radio and television. His awards include two Peabody Awards, an Emmy and ten Cable ACE Awards.

American businessman and computer scientist, co-founder of [[Google]]. With [[Sergey Brin]], Page developed the PageRank search ranking algorithm, for which the two received the Marconi Prize in 2004. He was chief executive of Google from 1997 until August 2001 and again from April 2011 until July 2015, when he became chief executive of the parent company, [[Alphabet Inc.]]. He stepped down from executive roles in December 2019 and remains an Alphabet board member and one of two controlling shareholders. He is among the richest people in the world.

Distinct juvenile form of many animals, occurring before [[Metamorphosis|metamorphosis]] into the adult. Animals with indirect development, such as [[Insect|insects]], [[Amphibian|amphibians]] and [[Cnidaria|cnidarians]], typically have a larval phase, and the larva is generally very different from the adult, as a caterpillar is from a butterfly. Larvae are often adapted to other environments; [[Tadpole|tadpoles]] live almost entirely in water, while adult frogs can live on land. Some larvae of immobile adults, such as [[Barnacle|barnacles]] and polychaetes, are mobile and use this stage for dispersal. In many eusocial Hymenoptera the larvae are fed by female workers. Some larvae, such as those of the [[Axolotl|axolotl]], become pubescent without developing into the adult form, a type of neoteny. The larval form does not always reflect evolutionary history, because in insects the larval stage often evolved secondarily.

1656 oil painting by [[Diego Velázquez]] in the [[Museo del Prado]], [[Madrid]]. Velázquez was the leading artist at the court of Philip IV of Spain. The work shows the five-year-old Infanta Margaret Theresa with her maids of honor, a chaperone, a bodyguard, two dwarfs and a dog. Velázquez portrays himself working at a large canvas, looking out toward the viewer, while a mirror on the back wall reflects the upper bodies of the king and queen. Its enigmatic composition raises questions about reality and illusion, and about the uncertain relationship between viewer and figures. Luca Giordano called it the "theology of painting". [[Michel Foucault]] opened *The Order of Things* (1966) with an analysis of its treatment of classical representation, and the painting went on to influence artists from Édouard Manet to [[Pablo Picasso]].

City (pop., 2024: 383,516), capital of the [[Canary Islands]], Spain. The city lies in the northeastern part of Gran Canaria, about 150 km (93 mi) west of Africa in the [[Atlantic Ocean]]. It is Spain's ninth-largest city. Juan Rejón founded it on June 24, 1478, and it was the de facto capital of the islands until the 17th century. The Canarian Ministry of Presidency is shared in four-year terms with [[Santa Cruz de Tenerife]]. In 1492 [[Christopher Columbus]] anchored in its port to repair his ship's rudder on his first voyage to the Americas.

City (pop., 2020: 641,903), most populous city in [[Nevada]] and seat of Clark County. Set in the [[Mojave Desert]], it is an internationally renowned resort city known for gambling, shopping, dining, entertainment and nightlife. Settled in 1905 and incorporated in 1911, it grew rapidly after Nevada legalized [[Gambling|casino gambling]] in 1931, the same year construction began on the tunnels of nearby [[Hoover Dam]]. Most of its best-known casino-hotels are on the [[Las Vegas Strip|Strip]], which lies just outside city limits. As of 2023 the city attracted over 40.8 million visitors a year, and it is the third most popular U.S. destination for business conventions. The name derives from the Spanish *las vegas*, meaning meadows, a term for fertile lowlands near local springs.

Stretch of Las Vegas Boulevard in Clark County, Nevada, lined with resort hotels and [[Casino|casinos]]. About 4.2 miles (6.8 km) long, the Strip lies just south of the [[Las Vegas]] city limits, in the unincorporated towns of Paradise and Winchester. Many of the world's largest hotel-casino resorts are on it, making it a major driver of the city's economy. The first full-service casino-resort on the Strip, the El Rancho Vegas, opened on April 3, 1941. [[Organized crime]] figures such as [[Bugsy Siegel]] financed the Flamingo, which opened in December 1946.

Analog home video format on [[Optical disc|optical discs]], the first commercial optical storage medium. Introduced in the U.S. in 1978 as DiscoVision, it was later rebranded LaserVision. Its 300 mm (11.8 in) discs stored an analog video signal, with CD-quality digital audio on many titles. Its resolution of 425 to 440 TV lines was nearly double that of [[VHS]]. Lack of recording capability and high player costs limited its adoption in North America and Europe, but it was popular in [[Japan]]. Pioneer ended player production in July 2009. The format laid the groundwork for the [[Compact disc|compact disc]] and [[DVD]].

Thermal manufacturing process using a focused [[Laser|laser]] beam to cut materials. The beam melts, burns or vaporizes material, and a gas jet often removes the debris. Computer numerical control (CNC) systems move the cutting head along a programmed path. Laser cutting was first used industrially in 1965, when a machine made by Western Electric drilled holes in diamond dies. In the early 1970s it was adapted to cut titanium for aerospace use and nonmetals such as textiles. CO₂ lasers are suited to cutting, boring, engraving and [[Welding|welding]], while Nd:YAG lasers provide very high power for boring and engraving. Suitable materials include acrylic, mild steel, [[Stainless steel|stainless steel]], aluminum and wood, though toxic fumes from PVC and ABS limit use. Tolerances can be as fine as 0.1 mm.

Most recent peak of ice-sheet extent, about 26,000 to 20,000 years ago, in the [[Last Glacial Period]]. Ice sheets covered much of northern [[North America]] and northern Europe, causing a major expansion of deserts and a large fall in [[Sea level|sea level]]. Average global temperature about 21,000 years ago was about 6 °C (11 °F) colder than today, according to the U.S. Geological Survey, and sea level was about 125 meters (410 ft) lower. [[East Asia]] remained largely unglaciated, because air masses created by the European ice sheets were too dry on reaching [[Siberia]] and [[Manchuria]] to produce the [[Precipitation|precipitation]] that glaciers need.

Period of major glaciation in the Late [[Pleistocene]], from about 115,000 to 11,700 years ago. It was the most recent glacial episode of the [[Quaternary]] glaciation, which began about 2.58 million years ago. It ended at the beginning of the [[Holocene]]. Glacier advance and retreat alternated during the period, with the [[Last Glacial Maximum]] occurring between 26,000 and 20,000 years ago. Canada was almost completely covered by the huge Laurentide Ice Sheet, while [[Alaska]] remained mostly ice free. The Younger Dryas, the most recent cooling, began around 12,800 years ago and ended around 11,700 years ago, marking the end of the period.

Hypothetical latest common ancestor of all current life, probably single-celled. Most studies suggest it existed by 3.5 billion years ago, and possibly as early as 4.3 billion years ago. All subsequent life descends from it under the three-domain system of bacteria, archaea and eukarya. No fossils are known, so its features are inferred from shared biochemistry and genomes, which suggest a complex life form with a lipid bilayer, the [[Genetic code]], and [[Ribosome|ribosomes]] that convert information from [[DNA]] to [[RNA]] to proteins. The term "LUCA" was first used in the 1990s.

Indian playback singer and occasional music composer. Born in [[Indore]], she began acting and singing in her father's musical plays as a child, and her professional singing career began after his death in 1942. She recorded songs in more than thirty-six Indian languages and a few foreign ones, primarily [[Hindi]], Bengali and Marathi. Considered one of the greatest singers of the [[Indian subcontinent]], she was called the "Queen of Melody" and the "Voice of the Millennium". The [[Government of India]] gave her the Dadasaheb Phalke Award in 1989, and she received the Bharat Ratna in 2001. In 1974 she became the first Indian playback singer to perform at the Royal Albert Hall in [[London]], and [[Guinness World Records]] listed her as the most recorded artist in history.

Societal collapse in the eastern Mediterranean and Near East, from the late 13th to early 12th century BC. It affected [[Anatolia]], Egypt, the Aegean, eastern [[Libya]] and the [[Balkans]], and it sharply reduced the material wealth of the region's powers. The palace economy of [[Mycenaean Greece]] broke apart into small, isolated village cultures, which were followed by the Greek Dark Ages (c. 1200 to c. 800 BC). The Hittite Empire collapsed, while the [[New Kingdom of Egypt]] survived in weakened form and [[Phoenicia|Phoenicians]] enjoyed increased autonomy. Causes proposed since the 19th century include climate change, droughts, disease, invasions by the [[Sea Peoples]], and changes in military technology that ended chariot warfare. Later research found that many destructions once attributed to the period were misdated or never occurred, so the collapse was more limited than once thought.

Mass extinction event of the [[Devonian]] period, around 372.15 million years ago, also called the Kellwasser event. It is one of the Big Five mass extinctions, though its severity is debated, with likely around 40% of marine species lost. A second extinction, the Hangenberg event, occurred about 13 million years later and ended the Devonian. Hard-hit groups included brachiopods, [[Trilobite|trilobites]] and reef-building organisms. [[Placoderm|Placoderms]] were hit hard by the Kellwasser event and died out in the Hangenberg event. Possible causes include changes in sea level and ocean anoxia, perhaps triggered by global cooling or volcanism, and a [[Comet|comet]] impact has also been suggested. Oceanic anoxia preserved organic matter, which, together with porous reef rock, made Devonian rocks an important source of oil in [[Canada]] and the [[United States]].

Mass extinction at the end of the [[Ordovician]] period, about 445 million years ago, and the first of the Big Five mass extinctions. It eliminated 49–60% of marine genera and nearly 85% of marine species. The extinction came in two pulses. The first, linked to a glaciation over [[Gondwana]] that shifted Earth from a greenhouse to an icehouse climate, destroyed habitats along continental shelves. The second came as warm conditions returned and was associated with worldwide anoxia. The extinction eliminated one third of all brachiopod and bryozoan families, and many trilobite, conodont, echinoderm and coral groups disappeared. Diversity recovered over the first 5 million years of the [[Silurian]] period.

Extinction of most of the world's [[Megafauna|megafauna]] at the end of the [[Pleistocene]]. Megafauna are typically defined as animals of 45 kg (99 lb) or more. Major extinctions occurred in [[Australia]] and New Guinea from about 50,000 years ago and in the [[Americas]] about 13,000 years ago, coinciding with the arrival of modern [[Human|humans]]. Overall about 65% of megafaunal species became extinct worldwide, rising to 88% in Australia and 83% in South America. Africa and Southeast Asia experienced more moderate losses. Most scholars support at least a contributory role for humans, through hunting, though climate change may also have contributed.

Transitional period between [[Classical antiquity|classical antiquity]] and the early [[Middle Ages]], roughly c. 250–750. It saw the end of the [[Western Roman Empire]] and of the [[Sasanian Empire]], the rise of the [[Byzantine Empire]], and the Arab conquests and formation of the [[Rashidun Caliphate]]. Diocletian reorganized the empire, and [[Constantine the Great]] legalized Christianity with the Edict of Milan in 313. The period saw the origins or ascendance of Christianity, Rabbinic Judaism and Islam, and the canonization of the Bible and the Quran. [[Justinian I]] codified Roman law. Historians once accepted the decline narrative of Edward Gibbon, but many now emphasize cultural renewal and adaptation.

Period of history after the early modern period, generally dated from 1789. Its transition was marked by the [[American Revolution]], the [[French Revolution]] and the start of the [[Industrial Revolution]] around 1760. Historians disagree on its end: some close it with the end of [[World War II]] in 1945, while others extend it to the present as [[Contemporary history|contemporary history]]. The [[Cold War]] is often treated as a subperiod, from the Truman Doctrine of March 12, 1947, to the dissolution of the [[Soviet Union]] on December 26, 1991. Other proposed labels include the [[Information Age]], which began in the mid-20th century, and postmodernity.

Machine tool rotating a workpiece about its axis, with tools applied to shape it. Lathes are used in woodturning, metalworking and glass-working, and can shape pottery, the best-known such design being the [[Potter's wheel|potter's wheel]]. Most metalworking lathes can produce most solids of revolution, plane surfaces and screw threads. The earliest evidence is a depiction in the tomb of Petosiris in the 4th century BC [[Ancient Egypt|Egypt]]. During the [[Warring States period]] in China, around 400 BC, rotary lathes were used to sharpen tools and weapons on an industrial scale. Precision metal-cutting lathes developed during the lead-up to the [[Industrial Revolution]], and the slide-rest, which guides the cutting tool to produce accurate cylindrical or conical surfaces, was a key advance. Lathes make objects such as screws, bowls, table legs and [[Woodwind instrument|woodwind instruments]].

Cultural region of the Americas, with [[Romance languages]] predominantly spoken, chiefly Spanish and Portuguese. Defined by culture rather than geography, it includes [[Mexico]], most countries of Central America, South America and the Caribbean, and [[Brazil]]. English-, Dutch- and other Germanic-speaking countries such as Belize, Guyana, Jamaica and Suriname are usually excluded. The term was introduced at a conference in Paris in 1856, when the Chilean politician Francisco Bilbao coined it for countries sharing a cultural and linguistic heritage. It gained wider use in the 1860s under [[Napoleon III]], whose government sought to justify France's intervention in the Second Mexican Empire.

Oral and written literature of [[Latin America]] in Spanish, Portuguese and indigenous languages. Pre-Columbian cultures were largely oral, although the Maya produced glyphic texts and the Aztecs produced codices, and the *Popol Vuh* was recorded after European arrival. Colonial writers included [[Bartolomé de las Casas]], whose *Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies* debated the ethics of colonization, and [[Juana Inés de la Cruz]], whose scientific writings included exchanges with [[Isaac Newton]]. Nineteenth-century novels, often called "foundational fictions", sought national identity. The 20th-century Latin American Boom brought magical realism to worldwide attention, most notably through [[Gabriel García Márquez]]'s *One Hundred Years of Solitude*. Jorge Luis Borges, [[Pablo Neruda]] and [[Octavio Paz]], the last two both Nobel laureates, exemplify its range.

Set of letters used by the ancient Romans to write [[Latin]], later augmented with lowercase letters for Medieval Latin. It evolved from the Etruscan alphabet, which came from Greek and ultimately from the [[Phoenician alphabet|Phoenician]] alphabet, itself derived from [[Egyptian hieroglyphs]]. The modern 26-letter inventory added W in the [[Middle Ages]] and separated I from J and V from U in the early modern era. The [[Latin script]] built on this set, often with diacritics or extra letters, is the most widely used writing system, serving over 3,000 languages spoken by about 70% of the global population.
